extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, literary critics, and general readers interested in literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Understanding and using Northrop Frye's framework (as presented in The Anatomy of Criticism) to read, classify, and evaluate literature, focusing on archetypes, genres, modes, and the ethical/social role of criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of criticism: construct a science of literature (not canon-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye: the goal of criticism should not be canon-making or politicking, but rather a properly elaborated science of the whole body of literature; 'Criticism, rather, is to art what history is to action and philosophy to wisdom: a verbal imitation of a human productive power which in itself does not speak.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should aim to build a conceptual universe in which literature can be systematically understood; avoid treating criticism as a tool for social/political gatekeeping. Emphasis on system-building and comprehensive conceptualization rather than taste-based selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical focus: criticism addresses rhetoric as expression of concepts and emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because no concept or emotion can be expressed without rhetoric, criticism addresses itself primarily to rhetoric and therefore to everything human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating literature, attend to rhetorical strategies (form, style, language) as the vehicle through which meaning and human experience are articulated; see rhetoric as central, not peripheral, to literary analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse adjudication of literary quality based on 'taste' or social prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye dismisses questions of literary quality as mere 'taste,' hence social prejudice, and argues criticism should refuse to adjudicate quality on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making evaluative judgments grounded solely in prevailing fashions or partisan taste. Distinguish analysis (structure, genre, mythic patterns) from moralizing or taste-based ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal/anagogic criticism: derive structural principles from myth and comparative religion
rubrics_metrics.description: The structural principles of literature are to be derived from archetypal and anagogic criticism, using symbolism of the Bible and Classical mythology as a grammar of literary archetypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use primordial images, mythoi, and religious symbolism as tools for revealing recurring structural patterns across literature. Treat myths and religious narratives as a 'grammar' that helps explain literary structures and recurring motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four central types of criticism (historical, ethical, archetypal, generic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye argues that the four central types of criticism—the historical, the ethical, the archetypal, and the generic—examine different aspects of literature that can nevertheless be reconstructed by the theorist as a unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these complementary approaches together: historical situates works in time, ethical considers social/ moral aims, archetypal traces mythic structures, and generic focuses on formal categories and conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four mythoi and their archetypal themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye's four mythoi: comedy, romance, tragedy, and irony; each has an archetypal theme: Romance—agon (conflict, sequence of marvellous adventures); Tragedy—pathos (catastrophe, triumph or defeat); Irony/Satire—sparagmos (sense of disorganization, defeat); Comedy—anagnorisis (recognition, rebirth, social renewal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing texts, map them onto these mythic cycles to understand their archetypal dynamics and how they relate to the life-cycle pattern (birth → death → rebirth). Use the mythoi as interpretive lenses rather than deterministic categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre taxonomy: distinctions within prose narrative (romance, novel, confession, anatomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye insists there are four genres of prose narrative—romance, novel, confession, anatomy—rather than treating all prose narratives as simply 'novels.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify narrative works according to these finer-grained genres to expand critical vocabulary and to avoid conflating different formal aims. Recognize the conventions and expectations specific to each prose genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge a work by the standards of the wrong genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye: 'we should not judge a romance by the standards of the novel and vice versa.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate texts by criteria appropriate to their genre/mode. Misapplied standards lead to misunderstanding and undervaluation; assess works within their formal and traditional contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical criticism: literature as a humanizing force and repertory for a just society
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 'Tentative Conclusion' Frye defines the study of literature as humanizing, providing students with a repertoire of images for an ideal or just society; 'The ethical purpose of a liberal education is to liberate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider literature's social and ethical functions: how works contribute to liberal education, imaginative freedom, and visions of a more humane community. Use ethical criticism to reflect on literature's civic and moral imaginaries, not to convert art into political propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of literature: protect literature's freedom from political instrumentalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye argues literature's autonomy legitimates its utopianism and that revolutionary action or political instrumentalization curtails literary freedom and human development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating literature or constructing criticism, be wary of reducing literary value to political utility. Maintain a balance between recognizing social implications and preserving literary autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to textual individuality and 'texture'; avoid over-generalizing by category
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics (Donoghue, Fraser) object that Frye's system often locates category at the expense of differences between poems and the 'texture' of poetry; Frye seldom quotes passages, which can leave readers short of the poetic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement archetypal/systemic analysis with close reading: quote passages, examine diction, musicality, and specific effects. Do not let typology replace attention to a work's unique aesthetic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: do not create works by strictly conforming to Frye's schemata (avoid formulaic myth-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that attempting to create great works by conforming to Frye's categories would produce formulaic, Campbell-ish myths (e.g., 'Star Wars'); 'it would probably result in Joseph Campbell, Star Wars, and other such simplistic stuff that piles up clichés and calls them myths.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Frye's categories descriptively, not prescriptively. Avoid engineering texts to fit archetypes; prioritize originality, complexity, and textual texture over schematic myth-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use taxonomy to expand critical vocabulary and understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye's lucid exposition of genres and modes 'expands our vocabulary for talking about novels, poems, plays, films, and other imaginative forms' and helps us value works for what they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ Frye's classifications as tools to increase appreciative and analytical precision. Learning the taxonomy enables critics and students to speak more accurately about form, tradition, and innovation.
